source_title: Carillion collapse: what went wrong? (House of Commons Library) - corroborated by NAO 'Investigation into the government's handling of the collapse of Carillion'
publisher_issuer: UK Parliament (House of Commons Library) and National Audit Office (NAO)
company_context: Carillion plc was the UK's second-largest construction and facilities-management/outsourcing group, holding hundreds of public-sector contracts (schools, hospitals, prisons, rail). It collapsed into compulsory liquidation in January 2018 after a chain of profit warnings tied to overstated construction-contract values.
business_type: Construction and outsourcing / facilities management (government contractor)
geography: United Kingdom (with overseas contracts in Middle East and Canada)
macro_context: UK construction sector with thin margins, aggressive competitive bidding on long-term PPP/government contracts, and heavy reliance on short-term financing and reverse-factoring (supply-chain finance) to flatter cash flow.
evidence_summary: Carillion's first major public warning came on 10 July 2017, when the board announced an £845 million contract provision (writedown) on a small number of material construction contracts, of which £375m related to the UK (mainly three PPP projects) and £470m to overseas markets (Middle East and Canada). The group had paid dividends and bonuses based on optimistic expected profits while debt mounted, a pattern the NAO and parliamentary committees characterised as aggressive accounting. It went into compulsory liquidation on 15 January 2018 with around £29 million of cash and over £1 billion of debt; the official receiver later estimated total liabilities of Carillion Construction at roughly £6.9 billion, including a pension deficit later assessed at about £2.6 billion (buy-out basis). The collapse cost roughly 18,000-19,000 UK jobs and the Cabinet Office estimated a government loss of about £148 million.
owner_decision_context: The board continued to recognise optimistic contract profits and pay dividends in cash while underlying cash flows on key construction contracts deteriorated, deferring the recognition of losses and relying on supply-chain finance and short-term debt rather than restructuring early.
action_taken: After the July 2017 £845m provision, the CEO resigned and the dividend was cancelled; the company attempted refinancing and restructuring talks with banks and government through late 2017. Talks failed and Carillion entered compulsory liquidation on 15 January 2018 (rather than administration), handled by the Official Receiver.
outcome_evidence: Compulsory liquidation on 15 January 2018; official-receiver liability estimate of c.£6.9bn for Carillion Construction; pension schemes entered the Pension Protection Fund; thousands of jobs lost and government incurred a c.£148m loss, confirming terminal insolvency driven by debt and contract losses.
source_limitations: WebFetch of parliament.uk and nao.org.uk returned HTTP 403; figures confirmed verbatim in WebSearch snippets attributed to the House of Commons Library briefing, the NAO report, The Pensions Regulator intervention report, and corroborating named journalism (Construction News, CNBC). Some figures (e.g., £6.9bn official-receiver liabilities) are post-collapse estimates and were refined over time.
directly_stated: 10 July 2017 board announcement of an £845m contract provision (£375m UK, £470m overseas)
Liquidation on 15 January 2018 with c.£29m cash and over £1bn debt
Official receiver estimate of c.£6.9bn total liabilities for Carillion Construction
Pension liabilities of c.£2.6bn as at 30 June 2017
Cabinet Office estimated government loss of c.£148m
inferred: Dividend/bonus payments based on expected (not realised) profits accelerated debt accumulation and masked solvency stress
Reliance on supply-chain finance flattered reported cash position relative to true working-capital strain
why_useful_for_opsiq: Canonical large-scale debt/solvency collapse where aggressive contract accounting and cash dividends masked deteriorating working capital until a single £845m writedown triggered insolvency. Tests whether the engine separates reported profit from cash solvency, detects debt-fuelled distribution, and routes a major writedown into governed re-evaluation of solvency and review cadence.
